name: Ruby laser

image.caption: Ruby laser rod and view through

lead: The ruby laser emits deep-red light at 694.3 nm. Theodore Maiman built it in 1960 as the first working laser, and it was among the first used in medicine, for tattoos and, from the 1990s, hair removal.

Ruby light is absorbed by melanin, so dark hair follicles and pigment spots heat up selectively, giving fewer dark hairs and lighter pigment. Studies in the 1990s reported follicle damage and hair reduction, and registered trials examined Q-switched ruby for sun-related pigment spots (lentigines). Wikipedia states alexandrite and Nd:YAG lasers have largely replaced ruby for hair removal.

paras: Today it is mostly a historical technology, and clinics typically offer newer wavelengths for hair removal. Hair removal with ruby used pulses in the hundreds of microseconds to milliseconds over repeated sessions, while Q-switched ruby uses nanosecond pulses for pigment and ink.

Because melanin in skin also absorbs 694 nm light, pigment changes and burns are recognised risks, especially in darker skin. Wikipedia lists ruby among lasers suited to paler skin types for hair removal.

angle.text: Ruby light is absorbed by melanin, so hair follicles or pigment spots are heated and the result is fewer dark hairs and lighter pigment. It is the first laser ever built and is now largely replaced by alexandrite and Nd:YAG for hair removal.

lead: The ruby laser is a solid-state laser using a synthetic ruby crystal that emits pulsed red light at 694.3 nm. Theodore Maiman built the first working laser, a ruby laser, at Hughes Research Laboratories on 16 May 1960. [1][2]

Ruby lasers were among the earliest lasers used in medicine, including for tattoo removal, and were later studied and marketed for hair removal and pigmented lesions. [1] According to Wikipedia, alexandrite and Nd:YAG lasers have largely replaced ruby for hair removal. [1]
Studies in the 1990s reported follicle damage and hair reduction with normal-mode ruby pulses [3][4], and registered trials examined Q-switched ruby treatment for solar lentigines [5][6].

paras: Maiman demonstrated the ruby laser in 1960. [1] Wikipedia credits Leon Goldman with early medical use for tattoo and scar treatment. [1]

A 1996 paper studied normal-mode ruby pulses (694 nm, 270 microseconds) for hair follicle destruction through selective photothermolysis, using dog skin ex vivo and human volunteers. [3] A 1998 paper in Archives of Dermatology reported on permanent hair removal with normal-mode ruby laser. [4]

In hair removal the ruby laser targets melanin in the hair shaft and follicle. Wikipedia lists ruby (694.3 nm) as suited to pale skin. [7] The same source notes that the U.S. FDA defines "permanent" hair reduction as a long-term, stable reduction in regrowing hairs rather than complete removal. [7]
A 1999 comparison of side effects of Q-switched Nd:YAG, long-pulsed ruby and alexandrite lasers for hair removal has been published, and indexed in the research literature.

Human studies include the early normal-mode ruby hair-removal reports [3][4]. Registered trials include a Phase 2 trial of side effects of Q-switched ruby laser for lentigines in light and dark skin types (NCT00386204, n=90) [5] and a small comparison of a Q-switched ruby laser versus a bleaching cream for solar lentigines (NCT02153697, n=15) [6]. Detailed results are not summarised here.

Wikipedia lists burns, hypopigmentation, hyperpigmentation, scabbing and infection among general risks of laser hair removal, noting that matching laser type and settings to skin type reduces risk. [7]
